scene.testo: Summer, 1945. Allied officers sit across a table from a captured German general. They have one question for him. Why did the Luftwaffe lose control of the sky over Europe? His answer takes only a moment.

The man is Adolf Galland. At thirty he became a general, one of the youngest in the German armed forces. He commanded the Luftwaffe's fighter force for more than three years. Few men knew the answer better.
He had flown in Spain, in Poland, in France, and over Britain. He claimed 104 victories in combat. And then he watched the force he commanded come apart, week by week, over Germany.
To understand his answer, go back to 1939. Germany began the war with one of the most modern air forces in Europe. Its fighters swept aside opponents in Poland, then in France. It seemed unbeatable.

Then came the summer of 1940. The Luftwaffe attacked Britain and met the Royal Air Force. The Battle of Britain was the first major defeat for German air power. Galland flew in it as a fighter commander.

Britain taught Galland a lesson he never forgot. German fighters escorted bombers across the Channel, but their range was short. Over London they could stay only minutes. Bombers paid the price. Remember that detail.

Within a few years the roles reversed. In 1942 the American Eighth Air Force began flying from England. Its four-engine bombers carried heavy machine guns and flew in tight formations. Americans believed they could defend themselves.

The theory was daylight precision bombing without fighter escort. B-17 Flying Fortresses and B-24 Liberators would fly deep into Germany by day. Their massed guns, planners believed, would hold off the German fighters.

At first, the theory seemed to fail. Through 1943, German fighters tore into the bomber formations. Pilots learned to attack head-on, where the defensive guns were weakest. American losses climbed, mission after mission.

On August 17, 1943, American bombers struck Schweinfurt and Regensburg. Schweinfurt made ball bearings. Regensburg built Messerschmitt fighters. The Luftwaffe rose to meet them. Sixty American bombers did not return from that single day.

On October 14, the Americans returned to Schweinfurt. Again sixty bombers were lost. Many more came home wrecked, with dead and wounded aboard. The Eighth Air Force halted deep missions beyond fighter escort range.

Inside Germany, the mood was confident. Hermann Göring, commander of the Luftwaffe, had once insisted that no enemy aircraft would reach the Reich. The record of 1943 seemed to support the boast. Galland knew better.

Galland saw something the public did not. Even in victory, his fighter force was bleeding. Every mission cost experienced pilots and aircraft. Germany was also fighting in Russia and the Mediterranean. Replacements were few.

Fighters were needed in the east, in the Mediterranean, and for the defense of the Reich itself. There were never enough. Galland pressed for more aircraft and pilots, and he pressed for priority at home.

Meanwhile, the Americans were solving their problem. Their problem was not the bombers. It was simply distance. Escort fighters of 1943 could not follow the bombers all the way to Germany's industrial heart.

The P-47 Thunderbolt was powerful, but thirsty. The P-38 Lightning had range, but engine trouble in cold air. Both fell short of the deepest targets. Then, in late 1943, another fighter arrived in England.

The North American P-51 Mustang began as a British request in 1940. Early models used an Allison engine and performed poorly at high altitude. Then engineers fitted it with a Rolls-Royce Merlin. Everything changed.

With the Merlin and drop tanks, the Mustang could fly more than 1,000 miles. Berlin lay roughly 570 miles from England. For the first time, an American fighter could escort bombers there and fight over the city.

In January 1944, Lieutenant General James Doolittle took command of the Eighth Air Force. He changed the escorts' orders. Fighters would no longer stay tied to the bombers. They would hunt German fighters wherever they found them.
The aim was not only to protect bombers. It was to destroy the Luftwaffe itself, in the air and on the ground. The bombers would draw German fighters up to fight. Then the escorts would be waiting.

In the last week of February 1944, the Americans launched what they called Big Week. Their bombers attacked German aircraft factories day after day. Escort fighters flew with them on nearly every mission. Some were Mustangs.

The Luftwaffe fought back hard. But its fighters now met American escorts deep inside Germany, in skies where German pilots had once flown unchallenged. The defenders were losing experienced men faster than they could train new ones.

Galland described the pressure in his memoir. Escorts hovered above the bombers and fell on German fighters as they climbed or formed up. Attacks that once reached the bombers now often failed before they began.
On March 4, 1944, a few American bombers reached Berlin, escorted by Mustangs. The weather turned most of the force back, but the message was clear. Two days later the Americans came in force.

On March 6, more than 600 American bombers flew toward Berlin with hundreds of escort fighters. The Luftwaffe attacked in strength. Sixty-nine bombers were lost. But German fighters suffered heavily, too. Only one side could replace its losses.

Galland's own account is blunt. He wrote that once American fighters could escort the bombers to Berlin, the day fighter force was in crisis. Losses mounted faster than training schools could replace them.

By his own account, the Luftwaffe lost more than one thousand fighter pilots in the first four months of 1944. Many were veteran leaders that no school could quickly replace. Fuel shortages shortened training further.

Now return to the room in 1945. Galland had been wounded in April flying the Me 262 jet and was captured. Allied officers wanted to know what had broken the German fighter force. His answer was written down.
The answer was not the jet. It was not Hitler's decisions, though Galland criticized them bitterly. It was not fuel shortages, which came later. The answer, in his account, was an American fighter.
The fighter was the P-51 Mustang. Galland judged it the aircraft that decided the air war over Germany. Not because it was perfect, but because of where it could go. Range changed everything.

He wrote that Mustangs over Berlin showed the Luftwaffe could no longer defend the Reich in daylight. Allied planners had long sought a fighter with that reach. Now it existed. The escorts had arrived.
Why did it matter so much? Because a fighter force cannot be rebuilt in weeks. Aircraft can be built quickly. Fuel can be found. But a trained pilot takes months, and a veteran takes years.

German factories did keep building fighters in 1944, in rising numbers. But new pilots arrived with too few flying hours and met experienced Americans. Many did not survive long. The Luftwaffe was losing its future.

The effects reached beyond the air battle. In Normandy in June 1944, Allied aircraft ruled the sky. German troops moved mostly at night. Later Allied bombing of fuel and rail targets met weaker opposition, and Germany's strength drained away.
By January 1945 Galland had been dismissed as General of the Fighter Arm after bitter disputes with Göring. He then led a small jet fighter unit flying the Me 262 against Allied bomber streams.

The Luftwaffe never regained the daylight sky over Germany. In May 1945 the war in Europe ended. Galland's answer stands as testimony. The bombers could not win alone. The escort opened the way, and the Mustang led it.

descrizione:
Why did the Luftwaffe lose the skies over Europe? In 1945, Allied interrogators asked Adolf Galland, the former General of the Fighter Arm, to explain the collapse of German air defense. His answer pointed to one American fighter, the P-51 Mustang.

This documentary follows the history behind that answer: the Battle of Britain, the Eighth Air Force bomber raids, Schweinfurt, Big Week, and the first escorted raids on Berlin in March 1944. It shows how long-range escort fighters changed the air war over Germany.

Built from real 1940s archival film and documented sources, this is WWII Testimony. Subscribe for more first-hand accounts from the men who lived the war.
